# Kaliyuga Bheema-Kodi Rammurthy Naidu

Kodi Rammurthy Naidu’s life reads almost like an epic tale of strength and service. He wasn’t just a performer of extraordinary feats , stopping cars with sheer muscle power or bearing the weight of an elephant on his chest , but a figure who embodied the idea of physical culture as a path to national pride. His titles , *Indian Hercules*, *Kaliyuga Bhima*, *Indian Sandow*, *Malla Marthanda* , show how contemporaries saw him as both a modern marvel and a mythic hero.

What makes him remarkable is how he fused athleticism with discipline and purpose. A strict vegetarian, he mastered yogic practices like *Vayu Stambhana* (air resistance) and *Jala Stambhana* (water resistance), blending traditional Indian techniques with modern bodybuilding. His circus company could have been just a commercial success, but he turned it into a vehicle for philanthropy and even contributed to the independence movement , channeling his earnings into causes larger than himself.

In a way, Naidu represents a bridge, between mythic archetypes like Bhima and Hanuman, and modern icons of strength like Eugen Sandow. He localized the global bodybuilding craze into an Indian idiom, making physical culture not just about physique but about moral and national strength.

### Early Life and Childhood

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Kodi Rammurthy Naidu was born into a Telugu family in Veeraghattam, Srikakulam district, to Kodi Venkanna Naidu. His birth date is recorded differently by sources — *The Hindu* notes April 1882, while *BBC News Telugu* and *Sakshi* mention 3 November 1883. His childhood was marked by both tenderness and hardship. When his mother passed away, his father raised him with care and affection, though Rammurthy’s restless spirit often led to clashes. Disinterested in studies, he once fled into the forests for a week, returning with a tiger cub — a daring act that foreshadowed his extraordinary destiny.

### Wrestling Beginnings

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

As a boy, Rammurthy was quarrelsome, and his father eventually sent him to Vizianagaram under the care of his uncle, Kodi Narayana Swamy, a police inspector. There, Rammurthy discovered *kusthi* (traditional wrestling) at a local fitness centre. His natural strength and discipline quickly made him an established pehelwan in the region, transforming him from a restless youth into a respected wrestler.

### Training and Rise

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

After schooling, Rammurthy was appointed drill master at his own school, continuing his training in his spare time. In 1901, he joined Saidapet College in Madras to study Physical Education. By 1911, he was performing feats that stunned audiences: breaking steel chains, stopping motor cars, and lying beneath an elephant as it passed over his chest. These demonstrations marked his emergence as one of India’s greatest strongmen.

### The Circus and Spectacle

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

With the help of his friend Potti Panthulu, Rammurthy established a circus company in Vizianagaram. His feats drew crowds from across India: breaking iron chains by flexing his muscles, halting cars tied to his shoulders, and bearing the weight of an elephant for minutes at a time. His circus became a national stage where physical culture was celebrated as a source of pride and inspiration.

### Recognition by the Viceroy

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Lord Minto, the Viceroy of British India, personally experienced Rammurthy’s strength when he attempted to drive his car against chains held by the strongman. Rammurthy held the vehicle back, leaving the Viceroy astonished. This incident spread his fame across the country, elevating him from a regional performer to a national icon.

### National and International Fame

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

At the Indian National Congress meeting in Allahabad, Rammurthy’s feats impressed leaders, including Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya, who encouraged him to perform abroad. Soon, he traveled extensively, performing across India and in London. His feats included stopping two cars driving in opposite directions at full acceleration, breaking half-inch iron chains, and balancing elephants on his chest.

King George and Queen Mary witnessed his strength at Buckingham Palace and conferred upon him the title *“Indian Hercules.”* His portrait was said to adorn the palace walls, and he became known as *“Kaliyuga Bhima”* and *“Indian Eugene Sandow.”*

### Triumphs Abroad

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Rammurthy became a regular performer in France, Germany, and Spain. In Spain, he was invited into a bullfighting ring. Though inexperienced, he seized the bull by its horns and threw it to the ground, earning admiration from the crowd. This daring act added to his legend, proving his courage in unfamiliar arenas.

### Patriotism and Philanthropy

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Rammurthy Naidu was drawn to the freedom movement through D. Chandrayya Naidu, who organized tribal youths against British rule. Though he earned crores through his circus, he donated much of his wealth to charity and the independence struggle. His philanthropy and patriotism elevated him beyond the role of performer, making him a benefactor of India’s freedom.

### Final Days

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In his last years, Rammurthy moved to the estate of his friend, the ruler of Balangir in Orissa. During the Sankranti festival in 1942, he met with an accident that claimed his life. His death in Balangir closed a life that had spanned from the forests of Srikakulam to the courts of kings and queens, from bullrings in Spain to the stages of the Indian National Congress.

## Legacy

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Kodi Rammurthy Naidu remains one of India’s most celebrated figures in physical culture. Known as the *Indian Hercules*, *Kaliyuga Bhima*, and *Indian Sandow*, he embodied strength, discipline, and service. His feats thrilled audiences, his philanthropy supported the freedom movement, and his legend continues to inspire generations as a symbol of resilience and national pride.
